title: Maximum Subarray / Kadane's Algorithm — running sum, reset when negative.
shortTitle: Maximum Subarray / Kadane's Algorithm — Running Sum, Reset When Negative

s1_definition.profdef: The Maximum Subarray problem finds the contiguous slice of an array with the largest sum. Kadane's Algorithm solves it in one linear pass by keeping a running best-ending-here sum and a global best. At each element you decide whether to extend the previous running sum or start fresh at the current element, whichever is larger, and you update the global best with the running sum each step. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India lists Rajesh's daily net cash flow, positive on credit days and negative on debit days, and an analyst wants the single stretch of consecutive days that produced the largest total gain. Walking day by day, you keep a running tally, but the moment carrying the past forward would drag you down below just starting fresh today, you reset and start a new stretch from today. You always remember the best stretch total you have ever seen.
s1_definition.oneliner: At each element take the larger of extending the run or starting new, and track the best run seen.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Maximum Subarray problem finds the contiguous slice of an array with the largest sum. Kadane's Algorithm solves it in one linear pass by keeping a running best-ending-here sum and a global best. At each element you decide whether to extend the previous running sum or start fresh at the current element, whichever is larger, and you update the global best with the running sum each step. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India lists Rajesh's daily net cash flow, positive on credit days and negative on debit days, and an analyst wants the single stretch of consecutive days that produced the largest total gain. Walking day by day, you keep a running tally, but the moment carrying the past forward would drag you down below just starting fresh today, you reset and start a new stretch from today. You always remember the best stretch total you have ever seen.

**One line to remember:** At each element take the larger of extending the run or starting new, and track the best run seen.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute force tries every start and end pair and sums each slice, which is cubic, or quadratic if you keep a running sum per start. Kadane's reduces this to a single linear pass by noticing that the best subarray ending at position i is either just the element at i by itself, or the element at i added to the best subarray ending at i minus one. You never need to look further back than that one decision.

You keep two values. The first, call it currentBest, is the largest sum of any subarray ending exactly at the current position. The second, call it globalBest, is the largest sum of any subarray seen anywhere so far. You initialize both to the first element. Then for each remaining element you set currentBest to the maximum of the element alone and the element plus the previous currentBest. If the previous currentBest was negative, adding it only hurts, so the element alone wins and the run effectively resets. Then you set globalBest to the maximum of globalBest and currentBest.

The reset-when-negative intuition is the heart of it. If the sum you have been carrying ever goes negative, it can only reduce any future sum you attach it to, so you throw it away and start a fresh run at the current element. This is why people describe Kadane's as "reset when the running sum goes negative", though more precisely you reset whenever starting fresh beats extending.

A senior point is the all-negative case. If every number is negative, the answer is the single largest, least negative, element, not zero. A naive implementation that initializes currentBest and globalBest to zero and only adds positives would wrongly return zero for an empty subarray. I initialize both to the first element so the algorithm correctly returns the least negative value when no positive subarray exists.

Another senior point is recovering the actual indices, not just the sum. I track a tentative start index that I move to the current position whenever I reset, and I record the start and end whenever globalBest improves. This matters in banking because the analyst usually wants to know which days formed the best stretch, not only the total.

For money I use BigDecimal with add and max via compareTo so sums are exact. A small finance-domain example: `BigDecimal cur=flows[0], best=flows[0]; for(int i=1;i<n;i++){ cur = flows[i].max(cur.add(flows[i])); best = best.max(cur); }` returns the largest contiguous net gain exactly.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India records Rajesh's daily net cash flow, positive on credit days and negative on debit days, and a performance-analytics feature finds the single consecutive stretch of days that produced his largest total net gain, to highlight his best financial run. The feature must scan long histories quickly. Finding the maximum contiguous subarray sum with Kadane's is exactly this.

This is exactly how Kadane's Algorithm works in Java — a running best-ending-here sum that resets when carrying the past forward would only hurt.

Problem 2 — Some months Rajesh is net negative every single day, and the feature must still return his least-bad single day rather than wrongly reporting zero, and all sums must be exact BigDecimal. This shows the all-negative edge case and money data-type care.

What the code will do: a `MaxSubarrayAnalyzer` with `bestContiguousGain(BigDecimal[] flows)` using Kadane's running sum with reset, tracking the best in BigDecimal. The demo finds Rajesh's best net-gain stretch.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the daily net cash flows are `-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4`.

Step 1: current and best both start at the first element `-2`, with the stretch anchored at day zero.

Step 2: at day one with flow `1`, extending gives `-2 + 1 = -1`, but the element alone `1` is larger, so we reset current to `1` and move the tentative start to day one. Best improves to `1`, stretch is day one to day one.

Step 3: at day two with flow `-3`, extending gives `1 + -3 = -2`, which beats the element alone `-3`, so current becomes `-2` and we extend. Best stays `1`.

Step 4: at day three with flow `4`, extending gives `-2 + 4 = 2`, but the element alone `4` is larger, so we reset current to `4` with tentative start at day three. Best improves to `4`, stretch is day three.

Step 5: at day four flow `-1` gives current `3`; day five flow `2` gives current `5`, best improves to `5`; day six flow `1` gives current `6`, best improves to `6` with stretch days three through six.

Step 6: at day seven flow `-5` gives current `1`; day eight flow `4` gives current `5`, which does not beat `6`. The loop ends with best `6` over days three through six, found in a single linear pass with only a few running values.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T18:30:00Z INFO Best gain = 6 over days [3..6]
2026-10-26T18:30:00Z INFO Best contiguous net gain for Rajesh = 6
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [-2,1,-3,4,-1,2,1,-5,4]  current=-2 best=-2
    │
    ▼
  each day: current = max(flow, current+flow); best = max(best, current)
    │ d1:1  reset  current=1  best=1
    │ d2:-3 extend current=-2
    │ d3:4  reset  current=4  best=4
    │ d4..6 extend current=3,5,6 best=6  (stretch 3..6)
    │ d7:-5 current=1 ; d8:4 current=5 (no improvement)
    ▼
  best = 6 over days [3..6]
    ▼
  Output: best contiguous net-gain stretch
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Maximum Subarray asks for the contiguous slice of an array with the largest sum, and I solve it with Kadane's Algorithm in a single linear pass with constant space. I keep a running best-ending-here sum and a global best, and at each element I take the larger of the element alone or the element added to the previous running sum. When carrying the past forward would only hurt, the element alone wins and the run effectively resets, and I update the global best each step.

The reset-when-negative intuition is the core. If the sum I have been carrying ever drops below what I would get by starting fresh at the current element, that past baggage can only shrink any future sum, so I throw it away and begin a new run. That single local decision at each element is why the whole problem collapses from a quadratic search over all slices to one linear scan.

The edge case I always call out is an all-negative array. The answer must be the least negative single element, not zero, so I initialize both the running and global best to the first element rather than to zero, which would wrongly allow an empty subarray. I also track a tentative start index so I can report the actual start and end days of the winning stretch, and I use BigDecimal with add and compareTo so every sum is exact.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to find Rajesh's best financial run, scanning his daily net cash flow to report the single consecutive stretch of days that produced his largest total net gain, even when some months were entirely negative. Explaining the extend-or-reset decision, the all-negative initialization, and the index tracking shows the interviewer that I understand Kadane's as a dynamic-programming idea, not a memorized trick.
